article.plain_text:
AI is expanding the centuries-old model of labor and capital into labor, capital, and intelligence. To achieve this, it requires an unprecedented infrastructure buildout that is breaking legacy corporate credit.
 Gartner exposes AI’s growing value gap
Gartner analyst David Furlonger further extrapolated, “The AI value problem will not be solved by simply adding more AI to existing ways of working.” In other words, if companies rely on AI to simply automate individual tasks then the economic upside is likely to remain limited and the pressure on executives will continue to increase. Instead, they’re going to have to think bigger. Enterprises will need to do the harder work of redesigning workflows, reimagining decision-making processes, and rethinking organizational structures.
 
The Economist: AI compute is the new oil—and needs a new market
The compute supply chain, then, looks ripe for marketisation. In the most simple form, chipmakers (like Nvidia and AMD) sell advanced AI semiconductors to equipment manufacturers (such as Dell and Hewlett Packard Enterprises), which package the silicon into racks and servers to sell to data-centre operators. Besides the hyperscalers, these include a few large “neoclouds” (one more linguistic innovation, denoting independent providers like CoreWeave and Nebius) and hundreds of smaller, less well-known firms.
American Thinker- When Money Dies: A Century-Long Prophecy
Elon Musk said it plainly on the Builders podcast with Walter Isaacson this month: “I think currency will be measured in fundamental physics metrics like, you know, power, like wattage and tonnage, mass and energy.” He argued that dollars won’t be the unit of measure in the future. It sounds radical. It isn’t. It’s a prophecy three of history’s most consequential minds made over a span of a hundred and twenty-six years, each from a different angle, each missing only the final piece. Bitcoin is that piece.
 
Over the past few weeks, a familiar chorus has taken over financial commentary: The bond market is cracking under the weight of AI capital expenditure.
Barclays warns hyperscaler capex is a “runaway train”
Goldman Sachs’ Jim Covello calls the $1 trillion infrastructure boom an economic dead end
Elliott Management cautions the entire trade is an overhyped bubble
Credit spreads are widening, tech giants are borrowing hundreds of billions, and the consensus says the debt-fueled party is over
Something bigger is underway as Wall Street is finally being forced to adapt to a genuine business revolution. The centuries-old model of labor and capital is now mutating into labor, capital, and intelligence.
Human Copy-Paste Machine
To understand why multi-trillion-dollar capital spending is rational, consider the modern white-collar job. Millions of knowledge workers spend their days acting as biological glue, manually shuffling data between incompatible ERP, CRM, spreadsheet, browser, and email applications.
Liberating humans from that friction with intelligence is only the opening act. As Gartner notes, 81% of CIOs are ramping up spending on machine intelligence, yet only 11% of CFOs see clear financial returns. Unlocking true value requires harder organizational work: redesigning end-to-end workflows, and even business models and corporate structures.
This potential overhaul, and the massive spend to make it happen, makes sense if we are adding intelligence as an equal to labor and capital. But it will also take more than addition; it will also take substitution.
When the iPhone arrived, consumers paid over $1,000 for it because it “substituted” cameras, GPS devices, music players, and voice recorders into one convenient device.
The enterprise software stack faces the same substitution/cannibalization. Today, corporations pay thousands of dollars per employee each year across fragmented SaaS subscriptions. An AI platform that restructures workflows directly across enterprise data lets CFOs eliminate those per-seat license fees. Capital simply shifts from bloated software rents to raw physical processing power.
When Technology Mutates Finance
Finance mutates because transformational technologies break existing instruments/institutions, leaving the financial system with no choice but to re-invent itself.
1171: Secondary Bond Market. Venice needed an armada of war galleys to fight the Byzantine Empire. The capital requirement broke traditional merchant pools, forcing the city to levy mandatory wealth loans (prestiti) with tradeable receipts, effectively inventing the secondary bond market.
1494: Double-Entry Bookkeeping. The expansion of multi-currency trade fairs rendered single-entry ledgers obsolete. Luca Pacioli codified the debit-and-credit balance sheet, establishing the foundation for modern accounting and corporate finance.
1602: Public Equities. Multi-year spice expeditions outgrew temporary voyage partnerships. The Dutch East India Company locked investor capital in permanently and issued tradable shares, inventing modern public equity and the joint-stock corporation.
1870s: Corporate Bonds and Credit Ratings. Transcontinental railroads required far more capital than local banks could absorb. Critics warned the railroad bust broke American banking, but the Panic of 1873 gave rise to equipment trust certificates, corporate bond syndicates, and the original Poor and Moody rating agencies.
1890s to 1920s: Utility Bonds and Capacity Contracts. Central-station dynamos and transmission lines required immense upfront capital before demand ramped up. Samuel Insull mutated finance by creating the regulated utility holding company and capacity billing, establishing modern project finance and utility bonds to electrify the nation, even if his holding company empire catastrophically collapsed in 1932.
In each era, commentators watched the old machinery strain and declared the emerging technology doomed. Yet every crisis catalyzed permanent, indispensable financial architectures.
How Finance Is Mutating Today
Today, public bond markets are balking at absorbing trillions in direct corporate borrowing on balance sheets. In response, capital markets are mutating along four distinct fronts to create an entirely new playbook:
Off-balance-sheet Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) are ring-fencing mega-project risk. If a hyperscaler borrows $50 billion directly to construct a gigawatt-scale datacenter campus, rating agencies threaten a credit downgrade and equity investors compress valuation multiples. Instead, tech giants are partnering with private credit titans like Blackstone, Apollo, and Ares to establish bankruptcy-remote SPVs. These entities raise billions in dedicated private debt, fund the physical real estate, and assume the construction risk. The tech company keeps the debt off its balance sheet, signing an operational lease for computing capacity once online.
Microprocessors (GPUs) are becoming bankable equipment collateral. Traditional banks treated silicon chips as an expensed asset that depreciated almost entirely over three years. Lenders are now underwriting multi-billion-dollar loans backed directly by warehouses of GPUs, modeled on 19th-century railroad equipment trusts. Because real-world rental rates for advanced silicon continue to outstrip standard accounting depreciation, financial engineers are calculating forward depreciation curves, secondary liquidation markets, and salvage values, turning compute hardware into a durable asset class.
Long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs) are replacing corporate promises as the ultimate collateral. An empty datacenter is just a concrete warehouse; it has zero economic value without a steady flow of high-voltage power. As a result, credit underwriters are underwriting twenty-year power contracts secured directly to nuclear reactors, natural gas turbines, and utility substations. The physical right to electricity, the literal watt, has become the foundational collateral backing the debt.
Raw compute is transforming into an exchange-traded commodity. The Economist noted that global spending on AI compute has already surpassed the global copper trade and is on track to rival the $2.3 trillion global crude oil market by 2030. Compute is evolving from bespoke contracts into a standardized, liquid market. Traditional exchange giants like CME Group and ICE are developing compute futures. Proprietary trading firms like Jump Trading and DRW are building dedicated compute-trading desks, while specialized market-makers write over-the-counter swaps guaranteeing fixed dollar-per-hour cash flows for server racks. Corporate IT spending is becoming a global commodity, complete with forward curves, hedging instruments, and central clearing houses.
Will It Get Messy First?
Financial mutations are never clean handoffs; they arise out of necessity, unfold chaotically, and routinely break legacy institutions.
Lenders can misprice GPU obsolescence, off-balance-sheet SPVs can hide excessive leverage, and datacenters can overbuild compute capacity. AI-related credit default swaps can flash warning signs that lead to market corrections, tempting skeptics to declare the entire technology an overhyped failure.
That skepticism is short-sighted. The desire to eliminate friction in knowledge work is too great to pass up (telling an agent to get data, make a chart, put it in a PDF, and email it to a group and update the CRM takes seconds; doing this manually can take an hour or more). This requires redesigning the modern organization and current business models. So, while this transition can be messy, and Wall Street may take some lumps, finance will be forced to rewrite its playbook (mutate) on the fly. That is the price of progress.
Strap in: institutions are evolving, finance is mutating, and the world is changing. The other side will look very different.

The Trump Administration's Project Uprise Is Accelerating America's Nuclear Renaissance Through Reactor Uprates, Restarts, and New Construction
THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION IS ACCELERATING AMERICA’S NUCLEAR RENAISSANCE
This week, Secretary Wright is visiting nuclear power plants in Illinois and Michigan to highlight the Trump Administration’s progress in expanding American nuclear power.
On Tuesday, October 27, 2026, Secretary Wright is visiting Constellation Energy’s Byron Generating Station in Byron, Illinois, to announce the Energy Department’s conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion to finance nuclear uprates and modernization across the midwest and northeast.
On Thursday, October 29, Secretary Wright will also visit Michigan’s Palisades Nuclear Plant, where the Energy Department is supporting the historic restart of a previously shuttered nuclear facility—the first ever such restart in the United States.
The Energy Department's Utility Power Reactor Incremental Scaling Effort (UPRISE) is advancing President Trump's nuclear expansion agenda by supporting nuclear uprates at existing reactors, restarting closed plants, and building new reliable nuclear capacity.
With the addition of Constellation’s projects, UPRISE has identified approximately 4.7 gigawatts of additional nuclear capacity—95% of its 5GW goal by 2029. The Energy Department is supporting the majority of these investments through loan funding from the Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF).
Under President Trump’s leadership, the Energy Department is delivering on President Trump’s Executive Order, Reinvigorating the Nuclear Industrial Base, to expand American nuclear power and strengthen national energy security.
The executive order directs the Energy Department to work with industry to facilitate 5 GW of power uprates at existing nuclear reactors and begin construction of 10 new large reactors with complete designs by 2030.
The order also directs the Energy Department to prioritize financing activities that support nuclear plant restarts, reactor uprates, completion of stalled projects, advanced reactor construction, and the domestic nuclear fuel supply chain.
UNLEASHING NUCLEAR POWER THROUGH UPRATES, RESTARTS, AND NEW CONSTRUCTION
Through EDF, the Energy Department is directly investing in advancing nuclear uprates, plant restarts, and new construction to expand America’s reliable electricity supply.
The Energy Department is supporting commonsense investments in additional capacity at existing nuclear generating units –the fastest way to get new, reliable power online.
Constellation Energy (Adding nearly 1.1 GW): Nuclear uprates and modernization across Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania will add enough reliable electricity to power more than 930,000 homes, backed by an October 2026 conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion.
Vistra (Adding 433 MW; Preserving nearly 4 GW): Uprates and modernization in Pennsylvania and Ohio will add new generation capacity while preserving enough reliable power for more than 3 million homes. This was supported by an October 2026 conditional loan commitment of up to $4.2 billion.
Vogtle Nuclear Uprates (Adding over 300 MW): Reactor uprates across 6 GW of existing nuclear capacity and license extensions for Hatch and Farley into the 2050s are expected to deliver more than $7 billion in electricity cost savings. In February 2026, the Energy Department closed a $26.5 billion loan package supporting these projects.
The Energy Department is supporting the historic restart of three previously shuttered commercial nuclear plants.
Palisades Nuclear Plant, Michigan (800 MW): The historic restart would return reliable nuclear power to Michigan’s grid and mark the first restart of a U.S. nuclear reactor that entered decommissioning status, supporting or retaining up to 650 high-quality jobs in Michigan, supported by a $1.5 billion loan to Holtec.
Crane Restart Project, Pennsylvania (835 MW): The restart would return enough reliable electricity to power approximately 800,000 homes and support more than 600 American jobs, backed by a $1 billion loan to Constellation.
Duane Arnold Energy Center, Iowa (615 MW): The restart would return enough reliable electricity to power nearly 500,000 homes, create approximately 1,500 construction and refurbishment jobs, and support more than 450 permanent operations jobs, backed by $1.9 billion in financing to NextEra.
The Energy Department is accelerating new nuclear construction to expand America’s reliable electricity supply.
The $17.5 billion American Nuclear Supply Chain Loans initiative is a conditional commitment that will help finance the equipment procurement for five eligible projects, with the goal of accelerating deployment of 10 new reactors by up to three years.
